evidence.text:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has been widely adopted in large language models (LLMs) since it reduces the computational cost through sparse expert activation.
However, the massive parameter scale of MoE models hinders their deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
Although existing mixed-precision quantization reduces the model size, they are inherently static, fixing the bit-width of each expert across decoding steps.
Such static schemes yield suboptimal performance as they overlook the dynamic variation in expert importance during decoding.
Furthermore, they fail to adapt to the dynamic latency constraint
driven by the fluctuating system utilization.
To address these challenges, we propose MatMoE, a dynamic mixed-precision quantization framework for efficient MoE inference.
MatMoE features: (1) a Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm that enables experts to operate flexibly at multiple precisions within a stringent memory budget; (2) a floor-and-compensation quantization method that eliminates redundant memory accesses in the Matryoshka representation; and (3) a dynamic bit-width allocation strategy that determines the precision for each expert based on their routing scores to satisfy the dynamic latency requirement.
We implement our MatMoE system atop llama.cpp for both CPU and GPU platforms.
Extensive evaluations across three modern MoE models and challenging benchmarks demonstrate that MatMoE achieves 4.0\%\sim 18.3\% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art static mixed-precision method.
Compared to llama.cpp, MatMoE delivers 1.3\times\sim 3.7\times speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, and 1.2\times\sim 1.3\times speedup on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and Jetson AGX Orin.

RAG is an advanced approach in natural language processing (NLP) that combines retrieval of relevant information from external sources with generation of new text based on that information ( Lewis et al., 2021 ; Izacard and Grave, 2021 ) . In RAG models, a retrieval component first searches for and pulls in related documents, knowledge, or data from an external database or knowledge base. This information is then fed into a generative model, which uses the retrieved content to create a more informed and accurate response or output. By incorporating RAG within an automated agent’s LLM, the agent can provide more relevant information, specific to its domain and use case ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Jeong, 2024 ) . This is particularly relevant when considering the application of automated LLM agents to the help desk and professional consultation industries. Because these industries rely on relevant domain-specific topic knowledge, RAG can be an effective approach to address the shortcomings of broadly trained LLMs. This is significant, as LLM-powered automated agents appear to be well suited to the work required in these domains. The help desk and professional consultation industries are broad and are present across almost all sectors of the economy. This includes customer support services, IT support services, administrative assistance, after-sales support and assistance, and several other types of support services. Although these service lines may appear to vary, they all rely on domain-specific knowledge, the ability to solve problems, and the ability to handle and mitigate errors to ensure that clients or customers have a good experience. Furthermore, they all rely on communication between a provider and a customer/client

Existing mixed-precision quantization methods for MoE models treat expert importance—whether measured by routing scores or activation frequencies ( Yi et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025a ; Duanmu et al., 2025 ) —as a static metric, determining it offline using a calibration dataset.
However, we find that the expert importance is inherently dynamic, changing significantly across decoding steps.
This is because of the specialization of different experts and the varying semantics of input tokens.
Notably, the load balancing loss used in MoE training is to guarantee sufficient and balanced parameter optimization across the training corpus, rather than to homogenize expert functionality.
Instead, it facilitates the development of highly specialized experts tailored to distinct knowledge domains ( Mu and Lin, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . As illustrated in Fig. 2a ,
expert ranking for the same expert varies significantly
across decoding steps even within a single sample.
The dramatic fluctuations of the routing scores in Fig. 2b further
demonstrate the highly dynamic nature of expert importance.
Consequently, this motivates a dynamic mixed-precision quantization method
that adaptively assigns the optimal bit-width
based on the expert importance at run time. Motivation 2: Stringent memory constraint and dynamic latency constraint on edge devices. Edge devices have limited memory capacity and dynamic runtime latency requirements since the system utilization fluctuates rapidly ( Kwon et al., 2025 ) .
Multi-scale quantization has been proposed as an effective solution.

Multi-scale quantization has recently emerged as a promising paradigm to address varying runtime constraints ( Kwon et al., 2025 ) .
It maintains a single quantized model capable of supporting inference at multiple precisions, thereby offering flexible accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.
Any-Precision DNN ( Yu et al., 2021 ) first proposes this concept in convolutional neural networks.
Any-Precision LLM ( Park et al., 2024 ) introduces multi-scale quantization to LLM, featuring a codebook-based non-uniform quantization and a specialized GPU software engine.
DP-LLM ( Kwon et al., 2025 ) further improves Any-Precision LLM by dynamically assigning different bit-widths to layers based on their relative quantization error.
However, the codebook-based non-uniform quantization incurs significant table-lookup overhead for weight dequantization.
Matryoshka Quantization ( Nair et al., 2025 ) proposes a uniform multi-scale quantization technique.
However, it requires an extra bit for rounding, diminishing the memory bandwidth saving.
Moreover, all these methods ignore the dynamic importance of experts in MoE.
A comparison of these methods with our MatMoE is presented in Table 1 . Comparison of existing multi-scale quantization works with our proposed method.

In order to enable experts to perform well at different precisions under the strict memory budget of edge devices, we propose the Matryoshka MoE PTQ algorithm, which consists of two stages. Stage 1: Determine the maximum allowable precision for each expert. Given a strict memory budget on edge devices, we first allocate the maximum allowable precision to each expert, aiming to minimize quantization loss while satisfying the memory constraint.
In contrast to PMQ ( Huang et al., 2025a ) , which relies on
a heuristic metric to guide bit-width allocation, we propose a more principled metric derived directly from the MoE layer’s output.
Specifically, the quantization loss of the MoE layer can be approximated using a second-order Taylor expansion as follows: where N is the number of activated experts, W_{i} is the weight of the i -th expert, Q(\cdot) is the quantization function, r_{i} and H_{i} are the routing score and the Hessian value
of the i -th expert, respectively.
Given the prohibitive memory and computational overhead of computing the exact Hessian matrix, we approximate it using the Fisher Information Matrix following ( Kim et al., 2023 ) as below: where g represents the gradient of weights and D is the calibration dataset.
Therefore, our proposed metric for each expert, i.e., r_{i}\cdot H_{i}\left[W_{i}-Q(W_{i})\right]^{2} , can be calculated offline based on a calibration dataset.
Based on this metric,
we determine the maximum precision allocation leveraging Integer Linear Programming (ILP) optimization, which only takes a few seconds to finish.

We design our MatMoE system on both CPU and GPU based on llama.cpp ( ggml-org, 2026 ) ,
which is the most widely used LLM inference engine for edge devices.
The overall system implementation of MatMoE is illustrated in Fig. 6 .
To facilitate efficient memory access for variable bit-widths, we adopt a bitplane-based representation ( Park et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2025 ) for the expert weights.
During inference, the execution precision of each expert is dynamically dictated by whether its routing score surpasses a pre-determined threshold (Sec. 4.4 ).
At the core of our compute engine, we develop highly optimized GEMV kernels tailored for both CPU and GPU platforms, as detailed below.
After the main computation,
we apply a lightweight compensation term to the
output of the low-precision experts (Sec. 4.3 ). On CPU, we develop a LUT-based compute engine.
The LUT-based GEMV kernel is first proposed in T-MAC ( Wei et al., 2025 ) for dense LLM.
During inference, it precomputes all possible products between the activation and all binary patterns, constructing a LUT.
The binary matrices of weights serve as indices to retrieve the precomputed results from the LUT, which are then accumulated to obtain the final output.
However, it does not support MoE computation.
To overcome this, we modify the kernel for MoE by introducing fine-grained, expert-level address offset control.
Furthermore, we share the LUT between the gate projection and the up projection of different experts to avoid redundant precomputation and storage overhead, since they receive identical input. On GPU, we develop our efficient GPU compute engine.
Since table lookup operation incurs severe memory bank conflicts on GPU,
we adopt a computation strategy fundamentally distinct from the CPU engine.

Multi-scale quantization has been proposed as an effective solution.
However, existing works are designed for dense LLMs, which exhibit the following limitations.
First, they adjust the precision at the model-level ( Park et al., 2024 ) or layer-level ( Kwon et al., 2025 ; Nair et al., 2025 ) ,
which incurs suboptimal performance for MoE models.
Second, they either lack an automated mechanism for determining the precision ( Park et al., 2024 ; Nair et al., 2025 ) or require a costly fine-tuning process ( Kwon et al., 2025 ) .
Consequently, this motivates us to develop a multi-scale quantization method tailored for MoE models with an efficient precision determination mechanism. Motivation 3: Redundant memory access in the Matryoshka representation. Although Matryoshka Quantization ( Nair et al., 2025 ) adopts a uniform quantization scheme to avoid the significant table-lookup overhead in Any-Precision LLM ( Park et al., 2024 ) and DP-LLM ( Kwon et al., 2025 ) ,
it has a fundamental limitation that relies on an auxiliary rounding bit, which inadvertently leads to redundant memory accesses.
For example, deriving a 2-bit quantized weight from a 4-bit weight requires fetching the 3rd bit to correctly resolve the rounding logic.
Consequently, 2-bit inference requires 3-bit memory access, degrading the theoretical speedup from 2\times down to 1.33\times .
Worse still, extracting 3 bits forces a full 4-bit memory access, completely neutralizing any potential throughput improvement.
On the other hand, naively truncating the first 2 bits will lead to significant accuracy degradation.
This dilemma highlights the urgent need for a novel quantization paradigm that secures accurate inference without the redundant memory access of the extra rounding bit.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture ( Dai et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Team et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) has been widely
adopted in Large Language Models (LLMs).
By dynamically activating only a small subset of experts for each token, MoE models achieve better scalability and performance than dense LLMs with comparable active parameter counts.
However, their large model size incurs substantial memory overhead, hindering deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization is an effective way to reduce the model size.
Compared to uniform bit-width quantization, mixed-precision quantization ( Dong et al., 2019 ; Dong et al., 2020 ; Yao et al., 2021 ) can achieve better performance under the same memory budget by selectively assigning higher bit-widths to the more critical layers.
Recent studies have focused on mixed-precision quantization on MoE models ( Yi et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025b ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025a ) .
They observe that experts are not equally important and assign different bit-widths to experts according to their importance.
However, these methods are static, i.e., determining the bit-width allocation strategy based on a calibration dataset and fixing it throughout the decoding steps.
Yet, we observe that the expert importance varies across decoding steps.
As shown in Fig. 1 , the static mixed-precision quantization cannot adapt to the dynamic importance of experts, resulting in suboptimal performance.
How to dynamically allocate different bit-widths according to the varying importance of experts remains an important open-ended question. MoE architecture and the comparison between the static and our proposed dynamic mixed-precision quantization.
